title: ‘ēlti — family and "my"
goal: Talk about your family, and attach the possessive endings that stick onto nouns — a backbone you'll use until the very last unit.
bekal: name family members and ask about other people's families
attach the eight possessive endings to any noun
use تَبَع as a second way of saying "whose"

dialogs.title: حَكِي — صُوَر عَ التِّلِفُون
dialogs.intro: Laila shows a photo of her family on her phone, and Budi replies with one of his own.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.literal: what God has willed. who this?

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.id: That's my dad. His name is Khalid.

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.baca: ēh, immi. w hadōl khayyi w ukhti.
lines.id: Yes, my mom. And these are my brother and my sister.
lines.literal: yes, mom-my. and these brother-my and sister-my.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: And your brother? What does he do?

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.id: He's a doctor at a hospital in Amman.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: Really? You have a big family.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: نِحْنَا تْلَاتِة بَسّ. أَنَا وْبَابَا وْمَامَا.
lines.baca: nihna tlaate bass. ana w baaba w maama.
lines.id: There are just three of us. Me, my dad and my mom.
lines.literal: we three only. I and dad and mom.

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.id: You don't have any brothers or sisters at all?

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: لَا، أَنَا وْحِيد. بَسّ عِنْدِي عَمّ وْعَمِّة كْتِير.
lines.baca: la’, ana wahiid. bass ‘indi ‘amm w ‘amme ktiir.
lines.id: No, I'm an only child. But I have lots of uncles and aunts.
lines.literal: no, I alone. but at-me uncles and aunts many.

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.id: Even better! May God keep them for you.

notes: **Possession is marked with an ending that sticks on, not a separate word.** English says "my house" in two words; Arabic glues it into one: بَيْتِي *bēti*. These eight endings are used through the rest of the book, so the table below is the most important one so far.

**Dad and mom have special forms when an ending is added.** The word أَب becomes بَيِّي *bayyi* ("my dad") and بَيَّك *bayyak* ("your dad"); the word إِمّ becomes إِمِّي *immi* and إِمَّك *immak*. The forms بَابَا and مَامَا from unit 2 never take an ending — they already mean "my dad", "my mom" on their own.
**Age is expressed with the word عُمْر, not with a verb.** The sentence عُمْرَا سِتَّعْش literally means "age-her sixteen" — no "is" and no "years". Adding سِنِة actually sounds like a textbook.

**The word خَيّ means brother, with no split into older and younger.** Levantine Arabic has no separate words for the two, just like English. If needed, add اَلْكْبِير ("the big one") or اَلزْغِير ("the little one").

**Saying مَا شَاءَ اللَّه isn't just a compliment, it's good manners.** When looking at family photos, children or anything lovely, Levantine speakers almost always say it — partly out of belief in the evil eye, partly out of habit. Skipping it feels cold.

**Long blessings in reply are normal, and you don't need to learn them all.** The phrase اَللَّه يْخَلِّيلَك يَاهُن roughly means "may God keep them for you". If you can't manage it yet, the reply اَللَّه يْسَلِّمَك *alla ysallmak* is always safe and always fits.

grammars.title: The eight possessive endings
body: Learn this table until it comes out without thinking. It works with any noun, and from unit 5 on it's also used to say "have" and "want".
after: Feminine nouns ending in ة change their ة into ت before an ending is attached: سَيَّارَة becomes سَيَّارْتِي *sayyaarti* ("my car"), مَدْرَسِة becomes مَدْرَسْتُو *madrasto* ("his school"). This rule has no exceptions.
In Lebanon you'll hear ـْكُن and ـْهُن pronounced more softly, almost like *-kon* and *-hon*. In Jordan they often become ـْكُم and ـْهُم, as in Fusha. All of them are understood everywhere.

grammars.title: A second way: تَبَع
body: For things that aren't part of you — things you bought, borrowed or just happen to be holding — Levantine speakers often use the word تَبَع *taba‘* instead of attaching an ending. It feels looser, and for beginners it's a safe way out when you forget the ending.
after: ⚠️ There's a limit, and it's what separates a natural speaker from a stiff one: **تَبَع is not used for family or body parts.** The phrase اَلْأُخْت تَبَعِي sounds odd, even funny, like "the sister belonging to me". For family, always use the ending: أُخْتِي.
The feminine form تَبَعِة and the plural تَبَعُون do exist, but in everyday speech تَبَع is used for everything. Don't bother learning all three.

blocks.text: Arabic distinguishes uncles on the father's side from those on the mother's side — عَمّ and خَال — and aunts too: عَمِّة and خَالِة. English uses one word, "uncle", for both, so this is a distinction you have to build from scratch. The good news: nobody in the Levant will misunderstand if you get it wrong; they'll just correct you with a smile.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Two words that can easily embarrass you
items: The word سِتّ *sitt* means **grandmother** — but it's also a respectful way to address an adult woman, a bit like "ma'am". Context makes it clear, so don't be afraid to use it.
The word مَرَة *mara* means both **wife** and **woman**, and calling a woman you don't know by that word sounds rude. To address someone, use مَدَام *madaam*, or آنِسِة *aanise* for a young woman.

head: Question
Say it
Meaning
rows: how many brothers and sisters do you have?

blocks.text: Questions about marriage and children come much sooner in the Levant than in most Western countries — often within the first ten minutes of meeting, from people you've only just met. It isn't nosiness; it's a way of placing you on the social map. A short answer is enough, and you can turn the question back.

blocks.title: Ready-made answers for questions that are sure to come
items: Not married yet: لِسَّا *lissa* — one word, polite, and it closes the topic gently.
Married: إِيه، مْجَوَّز *ēh, mjawwaz* (man) or مْجَوَّزَة *mjawwaze* (woman).
No children yet: لِسَّا، إِنْ شَاءَ اللَّه *lissa, inshaalla* — the answer you'll hear most, and the safest.
Her brother is a doctor in Amman.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.

answers: هَيّ عِيلْتِي. — اِسْم بَيِّي خَالِد. — قَدِّيش عُمْر أُخْتِك؟ — مَا عِنْدِي خَيّ. — بَيْتْنَا بِجَاكَرْتَا. — خَيُّو دُكْتُور بِعَمَّان.
بَيْتِي — اِسْمِك — عِيلْتُو — سَيَّارْتْنَا — مَدْرَسْتَا — شَنْطِتْكُن
جِدِّي — سِتِّي — عَمِّي — خَالْتِي — بِنْت عَمِّي — اِبْن خَيِّي
هَيّ عِيلْتِي. — قَدِّيش عُمْرَك؟ — مَا عِنْدِي خَيّ. — عِيلْتُو سَاكْنِة بِعَمَّان. — هَاد الْكْتَاب تَبَعِي. — عِيلْتِك كْبِيرِة كْتِير.
